entries.title: Sinhala at a glance
body: Sinhala is the language of the Sinhalese people of Sri Lanka, with about 17 million native speakers. It is Indo-Aryan, brought to the island over two thousand years ago, and has been shaped by Pali, Sanskrit, Tamil and later Portuguese, Dutch and English.
The verb comes last. Written Sinhala has verb endings for each person, but everyday speech drops them, so one form serves everyone.

entries.title: How Sinhala script works
body: Sinhala script is a round abugida; its curves are often said to come from writing on palm leaves. Each consonant carries a short a, other vowels are marks around it, and the al-lakuna ් removes the vowel.
Sinhala has prenasalized letters, such as ඳ (nda) and ඹ (mba), which are single sounds, as in හොඳ (honda, good).

entries.title: Spoken verb forms
entries.body: In speech one form serves every person. A question word turns -නවා into -න්නේ.

entries.title: Living things and things
entries.body: Sinhala separates animate nouns (people, animals) from inanimate ones. The verb for “be there” differs (ඉන්නවා / තියෙනවා), and so does “a”: කෙනෙක් for a person, එකක් for a thing.

examples.e: Have you eaten rice? (a common greeting)

entries.title: Sinhala and Tamil New Year
entries.body: Avurudu, in mid-April, is celebrated by Sinhalese and Tamils alike at the moment astrologers set for the sun's move into Aries. Families light the hearth, boil milk until it overflows, eat kiribath (milk rice) and play traditional games.
